name: Java
title: The Spice-Sea Empire
pitch: A navigator turns a young Javanese kingdom into a sea-trading empire, then reaches Australia's iron.

core.d: A fertile highland basin at ~450 m, cooler and less malarial than the coast, ringed by volcanoes and drained by the upper Brantas. The young kingdom (founded 1222) rules the whole Brantas valley from here.

start.d: The river port near the Brantas mouth where foreign ships unload; he arrives here with nothing. Its exact site is debated: some put it in Surabaya (Wonokromo / Kalimas), others further up the river near Mojokerto (~-7.42, 112.53).

facts: Population (region)
Java ~3–5 million (guess); Singhasari's Brantas core ~0.5–1 million (guess). No census exists before the 1800s.
Climate
Tropical monsoon. Lowlands ~26–28 °C all year; the Malang basin ~22–24 °C.
Rain
~1,500–2,500 mm a year, mostly November–April; May–October is dry. East Java and Madura are drier than West Java.
Growing season
All year. 2 rice crops where irrigated (3 in the best fields), plus dry-season crops.
Language
Old Javanese (Kawi) at court; Malay is the trade language of every port.
Writing
Kawi script on palm leaf (lontar), stone and copper plates. Literacy is limited to priests, scribes and nobles.
Religion
Shiva and Buddha worshipped together at court; village spirit cults; Islam only among foreign merchants.
Money
Chinese copper coins (imported by the shipload) plus local gold and silver weight-money.
Disease
Malaria on the coast and in the swamps, dengue, gut disease; the highland basins are healthier.
Big hazards
Kelud and Semeru volcanoes nearby; the Samalas super-eruption on Lombok in 1257; a Mongol fleet in 1293.

land.d: The royal heartland: deep volcanic soil, cooler air, much less malaria than the coast. Hemmed in by Arjuno, Kawi, Semeru and the Tengger massif.
The rice bowl of East Java: a 320 km river that loops round Mount Kelud and floods with volcanic mud. Old Kediri sits on its west bank; malaria in the low wet parts.
Swamps, fish ponds and river mouths facing the calm Madura Strait. The ports are here; so are the mosquitoes.

land.n: East Java volcano chain (Arjuno, Kelud, Semeru, Tengger)
land.d: Steep forested cones with fast streams (good for water wheels), sulfur vents and constant danger. Kelud's crater lake sends deadly mudflows down the Brantas.

land.n: Kendeng hills and Solo river teak belt
land.d: Low limestone and marl hills on poor soil, covered in teak (it grows best where there's a hard dry season). Oil seeps at Cepu and Bojonegoro.
Dry, flat limestone island with thin soil: bad for rice, good for cattle and for salt pans. Tough sailors.
Thinly settled forest and volcanoes at Java's east end, facing Bali. The Ijen crater holds a vent that lays down pure sulfur every day.

land.n: Southern limestone hills (Gunung Sewu) and south coast
land.rain: ~1,800–2,200 mm, but water sinks into the rock
land.d: Karst of a thousand cone hills and caves (bat guano, saltpeter), dry on top. The south coast faces the Java Trench: rough surf and tsunamis.

land.n: Central Java (Kedu plain and old Mataram)
land.d: The old heart of Javanese civilisation (Borobudur, Prambanan), rich volcanic rice land under Merapi. Less central to politics since power moved east in the 900s.

peoples.n: Singhasari court and the Malang basin
peoples.culture: Javanese rice farmers under a semi-sacred king, nobles and Shiva-Buddhist priests; temple building, gamelan, palm-leaf literature.
peoples.d: His patrons live here. The court was founded on a murder (Ken Arok, 1222) and King Anusapati fears the same fate.

peoples.culture: Dense wet-rice villages run by councils that share water; Kediri's old nobility, conquered in 1222, still proud.
peoples.d: The food engine of the realm and the place rice reforms pay off first. Kediri is the future rebel (1292); bind it in early.

peoples.n: Hujung Galuh and the delta ports
peoples.culture: Javanese harbour officials plus foreign quarters: Chinese, Tamil, Malay, Gujarati and Persian merchants. Malay is spoken everywhere.
peoples.d: His landing place. Foreigners are normal here, so he is just one more stranger; ideas also leak out fastest here.

peoples.culture: Seafaring Javanese, Chinese traders, fishermen and salt makers. Tuban is the main deep-water anchorage.
peoples.d: Second gate for big ships. Later (1300s–1400s) the first Muslim communities of Java grow here.

peoples.culture: Mountain farmers around the Bromo caldera, keeping old Shiva worship and fire offerings.
peoples.d: Healthy, cool upland country right next to the core. A safe retreat and a place for granaries above the mudflows.

peoples.culture: Javanese rice farmers of the old Mataram lands; famous temples, priestly families; loosely tied to the eastern courts.
peoples.d: Large population that can join peacefully when irrigation and trade reach it.

peoples.culture: Own language and kingdom (court around Galuh/Kawali in this period); more dry-field (ladang) rice and hill farming than the east.
peoples.d: Never conquered by East Java. A separate kingdom to deal with by treaty; controls the Sunda Strait pepper ports.

peoples.culture: Own language; cattle herders, salt makers, sailors and fishermen on a dry island. Tied to the East Javanese courts.
peoples.d: Raden Wijaya fled to Madura in 1292 in real history. Madurese sailors and cattle are an asset; the island's salt feeds the realm.

peoples.culture: Thinly settled Javanese-Balinese frontier; forest farming, hunting.
peoples.d: Controls the strait to Bali and the Ijen sulfur. Easy to win, hard to settle (forest and malaria).

peoples.culture: Hindu-Buddhist kingdom with its own court (around Bedulu); subak water-sharing groups run the rice terraces.
peoples.d: Model irrigation society. Kertanegara conquered Bali in 1284 in real history; Samalas ash falls here in 1257.

peoples.culture: Rice farmers under a small kingdom whose capital, Pamatan, lay near the Samalas volcano.
peoples.d: Pamatan is buried by the 1257 eruption. Survivors are the first big refugee wave, and he knows it's coming.

peoples.culture: Malay Buddhist port-state on the Musi river, once master of the straits, now fading behind Malayu-Jambi.
peoples.d: Its old role as the region's port of call is up for grabs. Its pilots and sailors know every reef.

peoples.culture: Malay Buddhist kingdom on the Batang Hari river; gold and pepper from the interior; the new leading Malay power.
peoples.d: Target of the real Pamalayu expedition (1275). Better as a trade ally than a conquest.

peoples.n: Malay states of the Peninsula (Kedah and others)
peoples.culture: Malay ports trading tin, jungle goods and rice; once Srivijaya vassals.
peoples.d: Tin and the Malacca Strait route. Small, easily drawn into a trade league.

peoples.n: South Borneo coast (Banjar area) and Dayak interior
peoples.popText: ~50,000–150,000 on the south coast and rivers (guess)
peoples.culture: Malay-speaking river settlements on the coast; Dayak peoples inland with longhouses, swidden rice and headhunting.
peoples.d: The nearest coal is in their hills (Pengaron). Trade and fair dealing with Dayak chiefs, not conquest.

peoples.culture: Malay trading port with close ties to China (Song records call it Po-ni); camphor and forest goods.
peoples.d: A stop on the China route and another Malay ally.

peoples.culture: Oldest Bugis kingdom in the Bugis tradition; rulers trade Lake Matano iron down the rivers to the coast.
peoples.d: Owns the nearest good iron. Already sells iron to Java for kris blades.

peoples.culture: Rice-growing chiefdoms, not yet the great sultanates; seafaring and shipbuilding traditions.
peoples.d: Future master sailors of the region. Natural partners for long voyages, and later for Australia.

peoples.culture: Clove-growing island chiefdoms (sultanates only from the later 1200s), rivals of each other.
peoples.d: All the world's cloves. Partner with both chiefs instead of conquering.

peoples.popText: ~15,000 before the Dutch massacre of 1621 (Willard Hanna); the 1230s figure is a guess
peoples.culture: Free merchant villages governed by councils of elders (orang kaya), no king; nutmeg and mace growers and traders.
peoples.d: The world's only nutmeg. A trading people who welcome fair buyers.

resources.qty: modern: ~320 km long, basin ~11,800 km², ~12 billion m³ of water a year (approximate)
resources.reach: 1230: already irrigates the valley through village weirs and canals; dams to control floods recorded as early as 1037.
resources.d: Water, transport and floods in one. Surveying and better weirs are cheap wins.

resources.qty: modern: one of Java's main rice areas; ~5–6 t/ha per crop today
resources.reach: 1230: ~1–2 t/ha per crop (guess), 2 crops a year where watered; row planting and drying the field mid-season could add ~a third.
resources.d: The surplus that feeds sailors, soldiers and refugees.

resources.qty: modern: small hand-dug sulfur workings on the Arjuno-Welirang summit vents (tonnage unknown)
resources.reach: 1230: crystals form at vents near the summit (~3,000 m); a hard climb but only ~20 km from court.
resources.d: The closest sulfur to the court. Enough for acid experiments; Ijen is the big source.

resources.qty: modern: ~14 t a day mined by ~200 porters, about 20% of what the vent lays down
resources.reach: 1230: pure yellow sulfur forms at the crater vent daily; carry it out in baskets as today.
resources.d: Plenty for sulfuric acid and blasting powder. Deadly fumes and an acid crater lake.

resources.n: Hill streams of the Arjuno and Kawi slopes
resources.qty: modern: many fast streams, several small hydro sites (exact flow unmeasured here)
resources.reach: 1230: steep, year-round streams beside the court; build water wheels on them.
resources.d: Power for hammers, bellows and saws right next to the capital.

resources.qty: modern: ~650,000 ha of teak plantation on Java; ~32,000 ha in the Randublatung unit alone
resources.reach: 1230: natural teak stands across the dry hills; float logs down the Solo river to the coast.
resources.d: Superb ship timber that resists rot and shipworm. Plant more from the start; teak takes 40–80 years.

resources.reach: 1230: Javanese masons already cut it for temples; river boulders everywhere.
resources.d: Building stone, millstones and dam stone.

resources.qty: modern: large river-clay deposits; Majapahit later built a whole brick city here
resources.reach: 1230: river clay along the Brantas; Javanese already fire brick.
resources.d: Brick and tile for fire-proof granaries and workshops.

resources.qty: modern: billions of tonnes; feeds one of Indonesia's largest cement plants
resources.reach: 1230: white limestone hills at the surface near the coast; burn it in kilns.
resources.d: Lime for mortar, soil, and later cement. Coastal, so it ships easily.

resources.qty: modern: Cepu field ~350 million barrels (Reuters); villagers still hand-dig shallow wells at Wonocolo
resources.reach: 1230: seeps and shallow pits; skim oil for lamps and ship pitch.
resources.d: Java's only real fossil fuel on land. Small, but useful for lamps, lubricants and caulking.

resources.qty: modern: millions of tonnes of black titanomagnetite sand along the beaches (exact tonnage not checked)
resources.reach: 1230: black sand on the beach; pull it out with a lodestone or wash it in pans.
resources.d: Hard to smelt because of the titanium (Japanese tatara did it). A stopgap until Luwu ore arrives.

resources.qty: modern: a very large copper-gold porphyry, roughly ~1–2 billion t at ~0.4–0.5% copper (guess from memory, not checked)
resources.reach: 1230: the copper lies hundreds of metres down; only some surface gold-bearing oxide is reachable.
resources.d: Mostly out of reach for now. Worth knowing for the far future.

resources.qty: modern: Indonesia's main salt island, hundreds of thousands of tonnes a year (approximate)
resources.reach: 1230: evaporate sea water in clay pans in the long dry season.
resources.d: All the salt the realm needs, for fish, meat and rehydration drink.

resources.qty: modern: hundreds of caves in the karst; guano tonnage not measured
resources.reach: 1230: dig guano and nitre earth from cave floors.
resources.d: Saltpeter for fertilizer and blasting powder. Far side of Java, so keep it modest.

resources.qty: modern: tens of thousands of hectares of brackish ponds around Sidoarjo
resources.reach: 1230: build pond walls in the tidal flats; stock milkfish fry.
resources.d: Protein for the coast; fish ponds also eat mosquito larvae.

resources.qty: modern: one of Java's busiest fishing grounds
resources.reach: 1230: calm, shallow strait fished from small boats.
resources.d: Food and a nursery for sailors.

resources.qty: modern: ~1 million Madura cattle on the island (approximate)
resources.reach: 1230: cattle and buffalo already pull ploughs and carts.
resources.d: Draft power, leather, and later cowpox for vaccination.

resources.qty: modern: small; replaced by sugar and imports
resources.reach: 1230: grown in the dry season on the drier east coast.

resources.d: Oil, rope, palm sugar for rehydration drink, and toddy.

nearby.qty: modern: 107 million t of nickel ore at 1.7% nickel (2023); the iron-rich red laterite on top covers many km² (iron tonnage not checked)
nearby.reach: 1230: iron villages on the lake shore (Pontada, Pulau Ampat) have smelted this ore since the 700s; buy bloom from Luwu.
nearby.d: The nearest good iron, nickel-rich (a natural steel alloy). About a week by ship plus river and lake portage.

nearby.qty: modern: part of ~33 billion t of Indonesian coal reserves, most in Kalimantan; the Dutch opened Indonesia's first coal mine here in 1849
nearby.reach: 1230: seams outcrop in the hills along the Riam Kiwa river, ~100 km up-river from Banjarmasin.
nearby.d: The nearest usable coal to Java. Ship it down-river and across the Java Sea (~3–4 days).

nearby.qty: modern: ~13.6 billion t of verified reserves in East Kalimantan (2021); many seams within 60 m of the surface
nearby.reach: 1230: outcrops on river banks; barge it down the Mahakam.
nearby.d: Huge and shallow. The long-term coal supply for the whole realm.

nearby.qty: modern: ~100+ million t of good bituminous coal (approximate)
nearby.reach: 1230: outcrops in the highland valleys, but far inland over the mountains.
nearby.d: Good quality, hard access. A backup source.

nearby.qty: modern: one of the world's largest tin fields (mostly alluvial and offshore); mined since the 1700s
nearby.reach: 1230: tin sand in stream beds; wash it in pans.
nearby.d: Tin for bronze, solder and tinplate. Easy to dig.

nearby.reach: 1230: a day's sail from Java's east end.
nearby.d: Hardy draft cattle and a second rice surplus.

nearby.qty: 1257: ~40 km³ of magma, VEI 7, column ~43 km high (Lavigne 2013; Guillet 2017)
nearby.reach: 1230: a quiet mountain; sulfur at the vents. After 1257, a 7 km-wide caldera and a buried kingdom.
nearby.d: Not a resource but the biggest hazard on the map. Fill granaries for a year of rice before 1257.

nearby.qty: modern: tens of thousands of small hardy horses (approximate)
nearby.reach: 1230: Bima already breeds and sells horses.
nearby.d: Pack and cavalry animals for Java. Tambora, on the same island, erupts in 1815.

nearby.qty: modern: mostly cut out by the 1900s
nearby.reach: 1230: thick natural stands; already exported to China.
nearby.d: A high-value export that pays for iron and coal.

nearby.reach: 1230: large stands in the lowland forest, floated down the rivers.
nearby.d: Extremely hard, rot-proof wood for piers, dock gates and bearings.

nearby.qty: modern: one of Indonesia's main pepper areas
nearby.reach: 1230: grown along the rivers and sold at the Sunda Strait ports.
nearby.d: The bulk spice that pays for trade with China and India.

nearby.qty: modern: cloves now grown widely; in 1230 these islands were the only source
nearby.reach: 1230: Javanese ships already carry them west on the monsoon.
nearby.d: The money crop. Partner with the chiefs; faster ships win the trade.

nearby.qty: modern: the VOC grew it on just ~46 km² of three tiny islands; the world's only source until the mid-1800s
nearby.reach: 1230: wild and garden trees on the islands; bought from Bandanese traders.
nearby.d: Worth more than gold by weight in Europe. Tiny, so whoever controls the trade controls the price.

nearby.n: Koolan and Cockatoo Island hematite (Yampi Sound, Kimberley)
nearby.qty: modern: high-grade hematite; BHP shipped ~68 million t from Koolan before 1994, mined on Cockatoo from 1951
nearby.reach: 1230: ironstone lies on the beaches (1800s pearlers used it as ballast); load it straight onto ships.
nearby.d: The closest Australian iron to Java, and it sits on the coast. Big tides (~10 m) and cyclones.

nearby.qty: modern: Rio Tinto alone holds ~2.7 billion t of reserves at ~61% iron (2022); mines like Marandoo grade ~62%
nearby.reach: 1230: red hematite hills at the surface, but ~250–300 km inland from the coast near Port Hedland, across dry land with little water.
nearby.d: The world's great iron field. Needs a road or rail and water wells before it pays; the coast is ~1,580 km from Surabaya.

nearby.qty: modern: ~47 billion t of black coal in the north Bowen Basin (Geoscience Australia); much is top coking coal
nearby.reach: 1230: seams outcrop in creek beds, ~150–200 km inland from the coast at Mackay.
nearby.d: Real distance ~4,100 km straight, ~4,700 km by sea through the Torres Strait (reasoned). Borneo coal is 4–8 times closer.

nearby.qty: modern: many billions of tonnes in the Sydney Basin (Hunter, Newcastle and Western coalfields; total not checked)
nearby.reach: 1230: seams outcrop on the coast at Newcastle (found that way in 1797).
nearby.d: Real distance ~4,800 km straight, ~6,000 km by sea (reasoned). Far too far for the first century; Borneo coal comes first.

newcomers.n: Lombok and Bali survivors of Samalas
newcomers.d: The eruption buries Pamatan and ashes Bali and Lombok. Rice farmers with the same faith and court culture; they fit Java almost perfectly if ships bring them and land is ready.

newcomers.num: ~5,000–30,000 over two decades (guess); records show officials fled to Champa and Đại Việt from 1276
newcomers.d: Shipwrights, iron-workers, potters, doctors and scholars from Quanzhou and Guangzhou. Chinese already live in Java's ports, but they keep their own language and ways.
Hindu seafarers and craftsmen with long ties to Java (a Cham princess later marries into Majapahit). Fit the court religion; different language.
Pilots, sailors and traders who already speak the trade language and share the Buddhist-Hindu court world.
Born seafarers and shipbuilders. They come for pay and land grants and are natural crews for the Australia voyages.

newcomers.n: Tamil merchant guilds after the Chola collapse
newcomers.d: Guild traders and craftsmen from Nagapattinam, already present in Southeast Asian ports. Share Shiva worship; keep their own community.
Bring cloth, glass, Arabic numerals and astronomy books. Different religion; they settle in port quarters and seed Islam on the north coast later.

newcomers.when: 1250s on, as new irrigated land opens
newcomers.d: Internal migration to newly irrigated valleys and to Bali and Lombok after 1257. Same or close culture; the biggest source of new hands.

neighbors.pop: ~60–80 million (guess-level; Song counts are by household)
neighbors.d: Rich, sea-trading, uses the compass; Quanzhou is the world's busiest port. At war with the Mongols from 1235 and falls in 1279. The biggest buyer of spices and source of crafts and refugees.

Took north China in 1234. Kublai demands Java's submission in 1289; Kertanegara scars the envoy Meng Qi, and ~1,000 ships with 20,000–30,000 men land in 1293. Typhoons wrecked their Japan fleets (1274, 1281).
Hindu sea kingdom on the Vietnamese coast, free again after Khmer rule (1203–1220). Wars with Đại Việt and the Khmer; invaded by the Mongols in 1283–85. Old friend of Java.
The Trần took the throne in 1225. Defeats the Mongols three times (1258, 1285, 1288, ending at Bạch Đằng). Proof that the Mongols can be beaten in hot, wet country.

neighbors.pop: ~2–3 million in the empire (guess); Angkor itself perhaps ~0.5–1 million
neighbors.d: Past its peak after Jayavarman VII (died ~1218). Rich in rice and stone temples; a declining land power, not a sea rival.

neighbors.n: Chola remnant and the rising Pandyas (south India)
neighbors.d: The Chola who raided Srivijaya in 1025 are weak under Rajaraja III; the Pandyas of Madurai overtake them and the dynasty ends ~1279. Tamil guilds still trade across the Bay of Bengal.
Malay-Buddhist port kingdom on the Malay Peninsula. Its ambitious king Chandrabhanu (inscription of 1230) invades Sri Lanka in 1247 and 1262. A rival for the straits.
The rising Malay kingdom of central Sumatra, heir to Srivijaya. Controls gold and pepper rivers. The real Pamalayu expedition (1275) went here; ally instead.
West Java's own kingdom, never ruled by the East Javanese. Controls the Sunda Strait. In real history Majapahit's attack on its royal party (Bubat, 1357) poisoned relations for centuries.
Ruled by the invader Kalinga Magha until ~1236, then a Sinhalese revival at Dambadeniya. Cinnamon, gems and Buddhist ties; fights Tambralinga's raids.

neighbors.pop: ~30,000–60,000 across the Top End, Kimberley and Pilbara (guess)
neighbors.d: Hundreds of nations with their own lands and laws, no farming, deep knowledge of water and country. No outside contact yet (Makassan trepang fleets start ~1700). Any iron coast must be negotiated with them.
